archetype.name: Retooling (volume-shooting, goalie-dependent)
archetype.definition: A Calgary team coming off a 28th-place season that controls enough of the puck to stay in games but lacks the chance quality, finishing and reliable goaltending to climb out of the bottom third.

report.headline: League-worst finishing luck hides a mediocre team, not a hopeless one
report.take:
Calgary sits 4-6-0, sixth in the Pacific and 27th of 32 on the site's Teams tab, a year after a 77-point season that ranked 28th. The surface numbers are ugly: a Goal Diff / GP of -1.6, 30th, with both the offense and the defense ranked 30th. Underneath, the picture splits. The Flames win their share of the puck, with a 51% CF % at 5-on-5 (13th) and 28.7 shots on goal a game (10th). The chances behind those shots are another matter. The xGF % of 46.8% ranks 23rd, so this is a volume team, not a dangerous one.

What has wrecked the goal column is percentages. The skaters are shooting 8.0%, dead last, against a league average of 11.3%. The team save % of .875 ranks 29th, and the all-situations PDO of 95.6 is the worst in the league; the 5-on-5 PDO is 93.5. The goaltending is really two stories. Devin Cooley has a .913 save % and +1.6 GSAx. Dustin Wolf has an .834 save % and -8 GSAx, 66th of 69 on the goalie tab, over the same five starts. Last season the Goalies GSAx was +14.2, and that cushion carried a team whose xGF % was 47% then too. For now it is gone.

The record also hides its own shape. The Flames lost the first five, including 1-6 twice to Seattle and 3-7 to Colorado. Since then they are 4-1-0, allowing 2.4 goals a game. Those early blowouts inflate the differential, which is why Pts vs Goal Diff sits at +1.7, second in the league. Special teams have been the lifeline: the PP % of 32% ranks 4th, the PK % of 84.8% ranks 7th, and 19 of the forwards' 45 points have come on the power play. A power play running well above the league's 21.2% will cool off.

The direction is up from here, but only so far. Shooting and save percentages this low don't hold, so goals should come back in both directions. But allowing 30.5 shots a game (29th) and losing the expected-goals battle put a ceiling on this group. It is close to last year's team without last year's goaltending. Whether Wolf returns to form, or Cooley takes the net, decides whether Calgary is a fringe team or a bottom-five one.

strengths.title: Special teams carrying the offense
strengths.body: The power play converts 32% (4th) and the penalty kill holds at 84.8% (7th), both well above league norms. Joel Farabee (6 PP points) and Matt Coronato (5) drive the man advantage. The kill looks more repeatable than the power play, which is running more than ten points above the league rate and will fade toward it.

strengths.title: Shot volume that should cash in
strengths.body: Calgary takes 28.7 shots a game (10th) and wins 51% of 5-on-5 shot attempts. Its 8.0% shooting is last in the league against an 11.3% average. Some of that gap is shot quality, since xGF % lags, but a team firing this much will score more than 2.3 a game once its finishing climbs off the floor.

strengths.title: Cooley giving them league-average-plus
strengths.body: Devin Cooley's .913 save % and +1.6 GSAx rank him 24th of 69 goalies, a functional NHL level. If that holds over a larger share of starts, the save % problem is partly solved from within.

concerns.title: Goaltending has flipped from asset to liability
concerns.body: The Goalies GSAx of -5.5 ranks 29th, after +14.2 last season and +16.7 the year before. That collapse rests almost entirely on Dustin Wolf's .834 save % and -8 GSAx. It is a five-start sample and likely to improve, but this roster has relied on its goalies to cover thin chance numbers, and without them there is no margin.

concerns.title: Too many shots, especially from centers
concerns.body: Calgary allows 30.5 shots a game (29th) and owns only 46.8% of the 5-on-5 expected goals despite winning the attempt count. That means the chances it gives up are better than the ones it creates. Opposing centers are scoring more above their norms against Calgary than against any team in the league. This is structural and won't regress on its own.

concerns.title: Thin grades across the roster
concerns.body: Forwards, defense and goalies all grade D. Zayne Parekh (-10) and Yan Kuznetsov (.403 xGF %) are getting buried in their minutes. No player is carrying a group, so a hot week from one skater won't change the profile.

trend.note: An 0-5 start full of lopsided losses has given way to a 4-1-0 run. Over that run the Flames allowed 2.4 goals a game, 1.5 fewer than their season rate, and the wins over Carolina, Minnesota and Detroit were all at home.

weekAhead.headline: Five games, three on the road, against teams outrunning their numbers
weekAhead.body:
The schedule looks rough on paper: Toronto (6th on the site), division-leading Edmonton, a Seattle team that beat Calgary 6-1 twice, and a Colorado side that put seven on them. But most of these opponents are living on finishing. Edmonton shoots 17.3% and Toronto 13.4%, while Seattle (43.3%), Toronto (45.2%) and San Jose (41.7%) all lose the expected-goals battle by more than Calgary does. A volume-shooting team with depressed percentages is a bad bet to keep getting blown out by teams like that.

The trouble spots are the Oct. 30-31 back-to-back, Seattle at home and then Colorado away, which will likely force both goalies into action. Toronto's kill, best in the league at 95.2%, also stands in the way of the one thing working for Calgary. A split of the five games is a reasonable target; anything better means the save % has turned.

keyMatchups.title: Power play against two leaky kills
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton (70%, 26th) and Seattle (70.6%, 25th) have two of the league's weakest penalty kills, and Calgary's 32% power play is built to punish them. Toronto is the opposite case, killing 95.2%. Expect the man advantage to decide the two division games more than the Leafs game.

keyMatchups.title: Edmonton's hot sticks, cold goalies
keyMatchups.body: The Oilers lead the league in goals and shoot 17.3%, but their Goalies GSAx of -8.5 is last in the league. If Calgary keeps its shot volume up, this is the likeliest game for its 8.0% shooting to come back toward normal.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle rematch after two routs
keyMatchups.body: Both losses to Seattle ended 1-6, yet the Kraken own only 42% of 5-on-5 shot attempts and allow 31.7 shots a game, 31st. On process, Calgary should control this game. The earlier scores reflect early-season goaltending and finishing more than a real gap between the teams.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal, and how often: Cooley's .913 against Wolf's .834 is the biggest single lever on Calgary's week.

restOfSeason.body:
The current pace of 66 standings points overstates how bad this team is. Shooting 8.0% and stopping .875 are both far below league norms, and both should rise. Even a return to an ordinary save % takes a goal or more a week off the against column. Working the other way, the 32% power play will drift toward the league rate, and the 46.8% expected-goals share and 30.5 shots allowed a game describe a below-average team. That profile closely resembles last year's 77-point club, which needed strong goaltending to get there.

My expectation is a finish of roughly 72 to 84 standings points: better than the pace, still outside the playoff picture. The upper end needs Wolf to return to form or Cooley to hold up as a starter. The lower end comes if the goaltending stays below average and the power play cools at the same time. Goals per game should climb into the 2.7 to 3.1 range as the finishing normalizes.
swingFactors: Dustin Wolf's recovery or a shift of starts to Cooley
How far the 32% power play cools
Cutting the shots and center production allowed

confidence.note: Ten games, an even goalie split and extreme percentages.
